IV. PERFORMANCE RESULTS
The registration method has been used to determine knee
kinematics in vivo in numerous studies involving hundreds of
patients and dozens of implant models [33]–[36]. Our results
are consistent with measurements made by other methods, including roentgen stereophotogrammetry [37], [38], intercortical
pins [39], [40], and quasi-static MRI [41], [42].
In this section, we give the results of tests performed to asses
the accuracy and repeatability of the method on in vivo and cadaver images. Many previous analyses of 3-D to 2-D registration methods have used “clean” images of objects outside the
body, or synthetic data [5], [16], [18]. However, to be sure of
testing the method fairly, the images should be as close as possible to those that would be clinically available. Specifically, the
implant components should be imaged within an environment of
bone and soft tissue, whose presence can affect the accuracy of
the results.
A. Convergence Analysis
Experiments were conducted to analyze the convergence
properties of the algorithm. First, a representative fluoroscopy
image was selected, containing a knee implant [Fig. 14 (left)].
Surface models were created for the femoral and tibial components. The best poses of the models were found (in terms of the
matching score), and are shown in Fig. 14 (center).
Note that these poses are not a “gold standard,” because we do
not know the true poses of the models from another, independent
measurement method. They are simply the poses which yield the
best value of the similarity measure. Therefore, the experiments
described in this section do not test registration accuracy, but
rather the ability of the search strategy to find the optimum value
of the similarity measure. Accuracy against a gold standard is
addressed in the next section.
Tests were performed to measure how well the registration
algorithm could find the best pose of the femoral component,

when it was run from different starting conditions. Four classes
of starting conditions were designated, representing different
amounts of deviation of the initial pose to the best pose. Class
1 represents the smallest amount of initial deviation, and Class
4 the largest. The classes correspond to the quality or accuracy
of the a priori knowledge of the pose. The actual initial deviation values for each parameter are shown in Table I. To set these
values, we performed an informal test. A human operator was
asked to manually position the femoral component model to best
align the graphical overlay with the image. Class 3 represents
the approximate deviation we measured after a few seconds of
manual positioning. Class 2 represents the deviation after about
a minute of careful manual adjustment. Class 1 and Class 4 represent even more extreme starting conditions—either very accurate or very inaccurate initial placement, respectively. An example, Fig. 14 (right) shows the model in its initial starting pose,
for one of the Class 4 starting poses.
1) Results—No Noise or Occlusion: Thirty runs were made
for each class. The algorithm was allowed to run unsupervised to
completion. For each run, the difference between the final pose
and the best pose was recorded. The root mean square (rms) final
differences are shown in Table II.
To test the effect of the random search component of the simulated annealing optimization algorithm, we repeated the runs
with the initial temperature set to zero. Effectively, with temperature equal to zero, the algorithm becomes a simple gradient
descent algorithm that just traverses downhill to the nearest local
minimum. We found, as expected, that the algorithm quickly fell
into a local minimum near its starting point. Thus, the algorithm
did not improve the initial pose estimate significantly.
A closer look at the results from full temperature optimization
shows that certain runs had large differences between the final
pose and the best pose. Nearly all of these incorrect final poses

efficient to use an interactive approach. In this approach, if the
system gets stuck in an incorrect pose, the user can temporarily
seize control of the model (using the mouse) and move it toward
the correct pose. Releasing the mouse then allows the optimization algorithm to resume at the new pose. This initializes the
state vector closer to the solution, saving time by reducing the
number of iterations needed to be performed.
This approach is a form of traded control [32], which is used
in supervised robot control. The philosophy is that the system
incorporates the best of both approaches. It combines the speed
and precision of the computer with the common sense and domain knowledge of the human. The resulting system is both efficient and reliable.

B. Accuracy Tests
The previous section showed that the registration method can
reliably find a pose that is very close to the optimal (as measured

by the matching score), even from starting poses with large initial errors. However, a separate issue is the absolute accuracy of
the resulting pose, in terms of 3-D translation and rotation. We
performed tests on a cadaver knee because it provided the same
imaging effects of bone and soft tissue that would be found in
in vivo images. The resulting images were completely equivalent
to in vivo images except that the objects were not moving while
the images were taken (however, if the exposure time is small,
motion blur is not a factor even for moving objects). We also took
images over a wide range of flexion and viewing angles, to simulate as closely as possible the range of imaging conditions that are
actually used in clinical X-ray fluoroscopy images.
In order to perform a test of absolute accuracy, we need a
source of known “ground truth” pose data. Ideally, the ground
truth data should be very accurate—at least as accurate as
the method being tested, and hopefully much better. Some
researchers have located fiducial markers (beads) in X-ray
images to obtain ground truth [19], [11]. However, since
our registration method itself is also based on X-rays, this
is not really an independent method. Other researchers used
mechanical positioning systems to place the objects at a known
relative pose [5], [16]. However, this method is difficult to use
on implants located within the body. Also, there are difficult
issues in calibrating the mechanical positioning system itself,
such as determining axes of rotation and the position of the
components on the actuators.
Instead, our approach was to physically measure specific
points on the implant to determine ground truth. In cadavers,
it is possible to expose a portion of the surface of the implant
so that it can be touched by a hand-held probe. The probe can
be automatically tracked using an optical sensor, and the 3-D
coordinates of the probe tip can be recorded by a computer.
Given a sufficient number of registration points measured
in this way, the pose of the implant can be estimated. This
pose can be compared with the pose that is estimated from
fluoroscopy images, as measured by our registration method.
One problem with obtaining ground truth is that it is difficult
to know the precise position and orientation of the fluoroscope
coordinate system with respect to the coordinate system of the
optical sensor. Even small errors in measuring this alignment
would result in large errors in the ground truth data, which
would dwarf the errors from our registration method. Therefore, we instead chose to concentrate on measuring the relative
pose between two implants (i.e., femoral and tibial knee
components), and compare the relative pose obtained using the
fluoroscopy registration method with the relative pose obtained
from the optical sensor. This avoided the need to calibrate the
fluoroscopy sensor with respect to the optical sensor. Also,
the relative pose between two implant components is often
the quantity of interest in applications such as measuring the
kinematics of the knee. However, one should note that our
test would unable to detect a systematic registration error that
would cancel out when computing relative pose.

IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON MEDICAL IMAGING, VOL. 23, NO. 5, MAY 2004

Improvement of Depth Position in 2-D/3-D
Registration of Knee Implants Using
Single-Plane Fluoroscopy
Takaharu Yamazaki*, Tetsu Watanabe, Yoshikazu Nakajima, Kazuomi Sugamoto, Tetsuya Tomita, Hideki Yoshikawa,
and Shinichi Tamura

Abstract—Two-dimensional (2-D)/three-dimensional (3-D) registration techniques using single-plane fluoroscopy are highly important for analyzing 3-D kinematics in applications such as total
knee arthroplasty (TKA) implants. The accuracy of single-plane
fluoroscopy-based techniques in the determination of translation
perpendicular to the image plane (depth position), however, is relatively poor because a change in the depth position causes only
small changes in the 2-D silhouette. Accuracies achieved in depth
position using conventional 2-D/3-D registration techniques are insufficient for clinical applications. Therefore, we propose a technique for improving the accuracy of depth position determination
in order to develop a system for analyzing knee kinematics over
the full six degrees of freedom (6 DOF) using single-plane fluoroscopy. In preliminary experiments, the behaviors of errors for
each free variable were quantified as evaluation curves by examining changes in cost function with variations in the free variable.
The evaluation curve for depth position was more jagged, and the
curve peak less pointy, compared to the evaluation curves of the
other five variables, and the curve was found to behave differently.
Depth position is therefore optimized independently of the other
variables, using an approximate evaluation curve of depth position
prepared after initial registration. Accuracy of the proposed technique was evaluated by computer simulation and in vitro tests, with
validation of absolute position and orientation performed for each
knee component. In computer simulation tests, root-mean-square
error (RMSE) in depth position was improved from 2.6 mm (conventional) to 0.9 mm (proposed), whereas for in vitro tests, RMSE
improved from 3.2 mm to 1.4 mm. Accuracy of the estimation of
the remaining two translational and three rotational variables was
found to be almost the same as that obtained by conventional techniques. Results of in vivo tests are also described in which the possibility of full 6 DOF kinematic analysis of TKA implants is shown.
Index Terms—Depth position, evaluation curves, independent
optimization, kinematics, single-plane fluoroscopy, 2-D/3-D

Improvement of Depth Position in 2-D/3-D
Registration of Knee Implants Using
Single-Plane Fluoroscopy
Takaharu Yamazaki*, Tetsu Watanabe, Yoshikazu Nakajima, Kazuomi Sugamoto, Tetsuya Tomita, Hideki Yoshikawa,
and Shinichi Tamura

Abstract—Two-dimensional (2-D)/three-dimensional (3-D) registration techniques using single-plane fluoroscopy are highly important for analyzing 3-D kinematics in applications such as total
knee arthroplasty (TKA) implants. The accuracy of single-plane
fluoroscopy-based techniques in the determination of translation
perpendicular to the image plane (depth position), however, is relatively poor because a change in the depth position causes only
small changes in the 2-D silhouette. Accuracies achieved in depth
position using conventional 2-D/3-D registration techniques are insufficient for clinical applications. Therefore, we propose a technique for improving the accuracy of depth position determination
in order to develop a system for analyzing knee kinematics over
the full six degrees of freedom (6 DOF) using single-plane fluoroscopy. In preliminary experiments, the behaviors of errors for
each free variable were quantified as evaluation curves by examining changes in cost function with variations in the free variable.
The evaluation curve for depth position was more jagged, and the
curve peak less pointy, compared to the evaluation curves of the
other five variables, and the curve was found to behave differently.
Depth position is therefore optimized independently of the other
variables, using an approximate evaluation curve of depth position
prepared after initial registration. Accuracy of the proposed technique was evaluated by computer simulation and in vitro tests, with
validation of absolute position and orientation performed for each
knee component. In computer simulation tests, root-mean-square
error (RMSE) in depth position was improved from 2.6 mm (conventional) to 0.9 mm (proposed), whereas for in vitro tests, RMSE
improved from 3.2 mm to 1.4 mm. Accuracy of the estimation of
the remaining two translational and three rotational variables was
found to be almost the same as that obtained by conventional techniques. Results of in vivo tests are also described in which the possibility of full 6 DOF kinematic analysis of TKA implants is shown.
Index Terms—Depth position, evaluation curves, independent
optimization, kinematics, single-plane fluoroscopy, 2-D/3-D
registration.

Yamazaki 2004 abstract and intro confirm:
- The depth position (z) is the weak axis: "a change in the depth position causes only small changes in the 2-D silhouette" — z is only weakly observable.
- The remedy is NOT gradient-type: "Depth position is therefore optimized independently of the other variables, using an approximate evaluation curve of depth position prepared after initial registration" — decoupled curve-fit z-polish, NOT a depth gradient, NOT geometry-based depth sensing.
- Results: RMSE depth 2.6→0.9 mm (sim), 3.2→1.4 mm (in vitro); other 5 DOF unchanged.
- "the evaluation curve for depth position was more jagged, and the curve peak less pointy" — the z-evaluation curve is jagged — important for the polish: the chamfer surrogate z-valley may be jagged/quantized.
- Simultaneous optimization via "nonlinear least-square method" — gradient-type for the 5 DOF + separate z curve fit.
- Biplane caveats: "limited space for testing, system complexity and increased radiation exposure remain unresolved".

content.thinking:
Yamazaki 2004 primary-text facts confirmed:
- Remedy is NOT gradient-type and NOT geometry-based depth sensing: it's a decoupled, curve-fit z-polish — "depth position is optimized independently of the other variables, using an approximate evaluation curve of depth position prepared after initial registration."
- The method: after initial 6-DOF registration (Levenberg–Marquardt nonlinear least squares — a gradient-type method for the 5 DOF + z jointly), move the model along the line joining the X-ray focus to the model's center of gravity, sample 10 depth points over mm steps, compute RMSD at each, fit a polynomial (order 4), find the extremum via Durand-Kerner root finding of the derivative, take the minimum extremum; then re-run the conventional 2-D/3-D registration a second time with the corrected z.
- Key mechanism quotes: "the gradient of the evaluation curve of depth position is much lower than those of the other 5 DOF"; "the evaluation curve for depth position was more jagged, and the curve peak less pointy"; "the gradient of the curve changed markedly with distance between X-ray focus and the model" — the z-gradient scale varies with focus distance → "it is difficult to find an appropriate scale for depth position" → the SAME_Z fixed weight problem, exactly as angle 03 R3-2 said.
- The z-curve's extremum is determined by apparent size ("position is primarily determined by the apparent size of the silhouette in the image" — Mahfouz; Yamazaki: movement along focus→COG line changes scale).
- 10 points, order-4 polynomial, extremum error saturated ~0.5 mm; RMSE 2.6→0.9 sim, 3.2→1.4 in vitro; residual bias ~0.5 mm attributed to in-plane→z coupling ("caused by slight errors in translation parallel to fluoroscopic images").
- "It would be difficult to determine a fixed weight value... because of the difference in gradient for each evaluation curve" (line 352-353) — the fixed-weight difficulty.

Important interplay with the round-1 z-depth-channel NO-GO: Yamazaki's remedy needs NO depth channel, NO DRR, NO gradient of a depth term — it maximizes the z information in the existing single-plane silhouettes by exploiting that z shifts = scale changes (movement along the focus→COG ray). This is consistent with the NO-GO (a depth buffer adds no target), AND it gives the polish a field-validated z-arm that doesn't fight the gradient scale problem. The yamazaki-polynomial mode of the probe (angle 03) is exactly this.

Also note: Yamazaki's movement is along the focus→COG line, not the camera-z axis — a nuance! Moving along the ray through the COG changes the silhouette scale purely (magnification), which is the maximal z-signal direction. The polish's z-axis perturbation (leaf z range) is approximately the same direction (the implant is near the image center, so camera-z ≈ focus→COG direction, differing by the off-axis angle). Worth noting in my analysis: the leaf-box z-axis IS approximately the focus→COG ray for a centered implant; for an off-center implant the scale-change direction differs from camera z by the off-axis angle — a small correction the polish could adopt from Yamazaki (perturb along the focus→COG ray rather than camera-z).

Abstract
Rendering bridges the gap between 2D vision and 3D
scenes by simulating the physical process of image formation. By inverting such renderer, one can think of a learning
approach to infer 3D information from 2D images. However, standard graphics renderers involve a fundamental
discretization step called rasterization, which prevents the
rendering process to be differentiable, hence able to be
learned. Unlike the state-of-the-art differentiable renderers [30, 20], which only approximate the rendering gradient in the back propagation, we propose a truly differentiable rendering framework that is able to (1) directly render colorized mesh using differentiable functions and (2)
back-propagate efficient supervision signals to mesh vertices and their attributes from various forms of image representations, including silhouette, shading and color images.
The key to our framework is a novel formulation that views
rendering as an aggregation function that fuses the probabilistic contributions of all mesh triangles with respect to
the rendered pixels. Such formulation enables our framework to flow gradients to the occluded and far-range vertices, which cannot be achieved by the previous state-of-thearts. We show that by using the proposed renderer, one can
achieve significant improvement in 3D unsupervised singleview reconstruction both qualitatively and quantitatively.
Experiments also demonstrate that our approach is able
to handle the challenging tasks in image-based shape fitting, which remain nontrivial to existing differentiable renderers. Code is available at https://github.com/
ShichenLiu/SoftRas.

SoftRas confirmed as a probabilistic-coverage formulation. Key facts for my survey:
- SoftRas = "soft" probabilistic aggregation over ALL triangles per pixel; gradients flow to occluded and far-range vertices.
- SoftRas's forward: probability maps Dj per triangle with soft coverage (sigmoid of signed distance), aggregate via softmax-like aggregation. It requires per-triangle depth sorting and per-pixel probability accumulation from ALL covering triangles.
- For JTML: implementing soft coverage means reworking the rasterizer's output semantics: instead of "last-writer-wins 255", each pixel accumulates probability from every triangle that covers it, weighted by depth. This is a fundamental rasterizer change (per-triangle contributions, depth ordering), not a ~10-line addition. Cost: high.

and engineering disciplines. Recent progress on differentiable rendering has
led to methods that can efficiently differentiate the full process of image
formation with respect to millions of parameters to solve such problems via
gradient-based optimization.

Nicolet "Large Steps" is about preconditioned gradient descent for geometry (vertex-position) optimization with meshes — the preconditioner (Laplacian-based) biases steps toward smooth solutions. Its subject is deformable geometry reconstruction, not rigid pose fitting. Relevance to JTML: the "preconditioned gradient descent" idea is about large steps in mesh-space; for a rigid 6-DoF pose, the step space is only 6-D — preconditioning matters much less, but the *large steps* idea for the badly-scaled z axis is relevant: the z axis's small gradient (per Yamazaki) is exactly the "different scales per variable" issue; a diagonal preconditioner (per-axis scaling, e.g., ADAM or a per-axis step-size) is the cheap transfer. Let me note: "our preconditioner biases gradient steps towards smooth solutions... each gradient step propagates information among all variables, enabling convergence using fewer and larger steps."

influence of geometric parameters on discontinuous regions of the

Ishit Mehta

Manmohan Chandraker

Abstract
We introduce a theoretical framework for differentiable
surface evolution that allows discrete topology changes
through the use of topological derivatives for variational
optimization of image functionals. While prior methods for
inverse rendering of geometry rely on silhouette gradients
for topology changes, such signals are sparse. In contrast,
our theory derives topological derivatives that relate the introduction of vanishing holes and phases to changes in image
intensity. As a result, we enable differentiable shape perturbations in the form of hole or phase nucleation. We validate
the proposed theory with optimization of closed curves in
2D and surfaces in 3D to lend insights into limitations of
current methods and enable improved applications such as
image vectorization, vector-graphics generation from text
prompts, single-image reconstruction of shape ambigrams
and multiview 3D reconstruction.

1. Introduction
Recovering geometry from images is a central theme for
several problems in vision and graphics, where a common
approach is to derive the differential of the rendering functional. Depending on the type of surface representation used,
such as Bézier paths [25], triangle meshes [10, 24] or levelsets [12], corresponding gradient flow equations are derived.
These works formulate image differentials as shape derivatives, which we posit to be restrictive for inverse problems,
since deformations induced by shape derivatives (SD) are
limited to surface boundaries. This may lead to local minima when recovering geometry with high-genus topology.
In Figure 1 we illustrate two inverse problems where shape
derivatives do not suffice to recover the optimal shape. In
such cases the optimization is required to make updates far
away from the boundary by (a) nucleating additional volume
in the exterior, and (b) perforating the interior of the shape.
Our work theoretically characterizes such shape perturbations in the form of topological derivatives (TD) for inverse
rendering.
We derive TDs following the definition proposed by

We observe that visibility terms in SDs are evaluated only

content.thinking:
DiffDRR (Gopalakrishnan 2022) confirmed:
- Reformulates Siddon's method as vectorized tensor operations in PyTorch, using autodiff.
- Rendering speed 73 ms (equivalent to CUDA/C++ DRR generators).
- KEY: "many applications use iterative gradient-free methods, such as the Nelder-Mead method [11], to optimize an image similarity metric with respect to the parameters of the DRR generator [3,13]" — the DiffDRR community itself used Nelder-Mead before gradient-based! This is a second independent primary text (2022, medical imaging) documenting Nelder-Mead simplex as the standard baseline for DRR pose/parameter optimization. This directly strengthens the simplex-polish arm argument.
- "we show that the loss landscapes for slice-to-volume registration in particular is convex in a large region around the optimum, making this problem better suited for gradient-based optimization methods" — the argument FOR gradient methods when the landscape is convex-ish near the optimum.
- The 'no torch in the cost path' boundary: DiffDRR's answer is "rewrite in PyTorch and use autodiff" — a fundamentally different engineering tradeoff than JTML's hand-written CUDA. BUT: the question is whether the DiffDRR family changes the boundary. My answer: no — DiffDRR exists BECAUSE the CUDA/C++ DRR generators "do not offer a straightforward way to obtain gradients"; JTML's polish has an analytic closed-form gradient (the 2×6 projection Jacobian) that needs no autodiff — the analytic route IS the "no torch" answer to the same problem DiffDRR solves with torch. And the DRR forward + z-line-integral channel: DiffDRR shows it's differentiable via autodiff in torch; a hand-written CUDA version would need the analytic Jacobian of the ray-casting — doable but delicate (round-1 NO-GO for the photometric route stands on the saturated-implant intensity issue, not on differentiability).
- Also: "Most open-source CPU-based implementations take about 1 sec to generate a single DRR... GPU-accelerated DRR generators... 100 msec" — a DRR render is ~73 ms, i.e., ~10× slower than JTML's silhouette render presumably. Not directly load-bearing.

Let me also grep the DiffDRR text for the "no torch" angle — e.g., their custom CUDA op (they have a pure-PyTorch and a CUDA op version). Let me quickly grep for "custom" / "CUDA".

DiffDRR text confirmed with rich detail:
- Nelder-Mead was THE standard gradient-free optimizer for DRR parameter optimization (cites [3,13] and Singer & Nelder's Scholarpedia).
- "the loss landscapes for slice-to-volume registration in particular is convex in a large region around the optimum" — locally convex loss → gradient methods better.
- They used per-axis update rates: "We used different update rates for the rotational and translational parameters because they have different units (βθϕγ = 5.3×10^-2 and βxyz = 7.5×10^1), and momentum λ = 0.9" — primary-text confirmation of the per-axis scaling necessity (the MVP's h·sign(g) and ADAM-lite), same unit-mixing issue as JTML's z vs in-plane.
- 6-DoF DRR registration with gradient descent, 250 iterations.
- Also: DRR generators in CUDA/C++ "do not offer a straightforward way to obtain gradients" → their torch rewrite. And DeepDRR for scattering realism.

Now Bangaru 2022 (Differentiable Rendering of Neural SDFs through Reparameterization). Let me read.

INTRODUCTION

Differentiable rendering algorithms have become crucial tools in
solving challenging inverse problems [Zhao et al. 2020], thanks to
their ability to compute the derivatives of images with respect to
arbitrary scene parameters. Naive differentiation of rendering algorithms does not handle discontinuities caused by visibility changes
and object boundaries correctly. Previous work has observed that
the discontinuities can be handled by properly handling the Dirac
delta signals, and derived algorithms for explicit geometry representations like triangle meshes [Li et al. 2018; Zhang et al. 2020].
On the other hand, implicit representations like signed distance
fields (SDFs) are appealing since they do not require the initialized
geometry to have the right topology. Recent work has demonstrated
the use of SDFs—usually parameterized using multi-layer perceptron networks—for the task of reconstructing shape and surface

reflectance from images. However, these methods either require additional geometric supervision such as segmentation masks [Yariv
et al. 2020; Zhang et al. 2021b] or make approximations to the geometry using volumetric models [Oechsle et al. 2021; Yariv et al. 2021]
that limit their applicability.
In this paper, we derive an algorithm to automatically compute
correct gradients with respect to geometric scene parameters in
neural SDF renderers. Previous methods that rely on silhouette
sampling are not directly applicable to SDFs since direct sampling of
boundaries of implicit functions is challenging. Instead, we build on
the reparameterization approaches [Bangaru et al. 2020; Loubet et al.
2019], which removes discontinuities through reparameterization
while preserving the integral values. These methods do not require
explicit sampling along discontinuities. Previous reparameterization
methods focused on triangle meshes, and require new derivation
for reparameterizing SDF rendering.
Specifically, we construct a silhouette-aware reparameterization
similar to that of Loubet et al. [2019], but following the equivalent
unbiased warp definition that Bangaru et al. [2020] used to produce
correct gradients for triangle-meshes. We leverage the fact that
SDFs naturally encode the distance to the surface, and develop a
practical algorithm that uses a quadrature on sphere tracing [Hart
1996] samples to construct a reparameterization that removes the
discontinuities. We further show that this can be computed using

Differentiable rendering algorithms have become crucial tools in
solving challenging inverse problems [Zhao et al. 2020], thanks to
their ability to compute the derivatives of images with respect to
arbitrary scene parameters. Naive differentiation of rendering algorithms does not handle discontinuities caused by visibility changes
and object boundaries correctly. Previous work has observed that
the discontinuities can be handled by properly handling the Dirac
delta signals, and derived algorithms for explicit geometry representations like triangle meshes [Li et al. 2018; Zhang et al. 2020].
On the other hand, implicit representations like signed distance
fields (SDFs) are appealing since they do not require the initialized
geometry to have the right topology. Recent work has demonstrated
the use of SDFs—usually parameterized using multi-layer perceptron networks—for the task of reconstructing shape and surface

that limit their applicability.

Bangaru 2022 = neural SDF reparameterization for PBR (sphere tracing, warp functions, quadrature) — requires SDF representation + sphere tracing. For JTML: the implant is a fixed STL mesh; converting to an SDF and ray-marching for a 6-DoF pose polish is much heavier machinery than the analytic silhouette gradient. Not the cheapest. The reparameterization/warp idea is the PBR-side cousin of SoftRas-style smoothing. Relevance: low for the MVP; it's the "SDF reparameterization" strategy named in the dispatch — verdict: not cheapest for a mesh rasterizer; the SDF route only makes sense if the geometry were being deformed or if the mask-free multi-view reconstruction were the goal.

Now Zhang 2020 (Path-Space Differentiable Rendering). Let me read the abstract/intro briefly, since it's the "pathspace" strategy in the dispatch.

The zhangPathspaceDifferentiableRendering2020.txt is actually Cheng Zhang's PhD dissertation "Path-Space Differentiable Rendering" (UC Irvine, 2022) — the PSDR (path-space differentiable rendering) work — Monte Carlo light transport with boundary sampling ("from the middle" paths tangent to mesh edges). This is the light-transport boundary-sampling family. For JTML: not applicable to silhouette/X-ray registration — it's for global illumination. In the survey: the "pathspace" strategy is the most expensive and least relevant (requires MC light transport).

The zhangPathspaceDifferentiableRendering2020.txt is actually the PSDR dissertation (Zhang, Cheng, UC Irvine 2022 — the published form of "Path-Space Differentiable Rendering" SIGGRAPH 2020 paper). Confirmed: Monte Carlo boundary integrals via edge-sampling for light transport; "All of these edge-sampling techniques do not scale well to complex geometry due to the necessity for run-time silhouette detection." — interesting: silhouette detection is the bottleneck even in PBR. For JTML: the boundary term in the MVP's analytic gradient is exactly the "boundary integral" concept (pixels entering/leaving the EDGE set); the PSDR family gives the theory (interior term + boundary term decomposition; Eq. 2.36), but the machinery (MC light transport) doesn't apply to rasterization. Verdict: theory-relevant for the boundary-term question (confirms the decomposition), implementation-irrelevant.

IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON MEDICAL IMAGING, VOL. 22, NO. 11, NOVEMBER 2003

Gradient-Based 2-D/3-D Rigid Registration of
Fluoroscopic X-Ray to CT
Harel Livyatan, Ziv Yaniv, Student Member, IEEE, and Leo Joskowicz*, Senior Member, IEEE

Abstract—We present a gradient-based method for rigid registration of a patient preoperative computed tomography (CT) to its
intraoperative situation with a few fluoroscopic X-ray images obtained with a tracked C-arm. The method is noninvasive, anatomybased, requires simple user interaction, and includes validation. It
is generic and easily customizable for a variety of routine clinical
uses in orthopaedic surgery. Gradient-based registration consists
of three steps: 1) initial pose estimation; 2) coarse geometry-based
registration on bone contours, and; 3) fine gradient projection registration (GPR) on edge pixels. It optimizes speed, accuracy, and
robustness. Its novelty resides in using volume gradients to eliminate outliers and foreign objects in the fluoroscopic X-ray images,
in speeding up computation, and in achieving higher accuracy. It
overcomes the drawbacks of intensity-based methods, which are
slow and have a limited convergence range, and of geometry-based
methods, which depend on the image segmentation quality. Our
simulated, in vitro, and cadaver experiments on a human pelvis
CT, dry vertebra, dry femur, fresh lamb hip, and human pelvis
under realistic conditions show a mean 0.5–1.7 mm (0.5–2.6 mm
maximum) target registration accuracy.
Index Terms—Fluoroscopic X-ray to CT registration, gradient
based, image registration, 2D/3D rigid registration.

I. INTRODUCTION

R

EGISTRATION is the task of finding a transformation
from the coordinate system of one data set to another
so that all features that appear in both data sets are aligned.
Registration is an essential step in most computer-aided surgery
(CAS) systems, since it is necessary to match information
from different data modalities obtained at different times. In
image-guided surgery, it is required to match the preoperative
images and plans to the intraoperative situation, and to determine the relative positions of surgical tools and anatomical
structures. Examples of deployed CAS systems include preoperative planning, intraoperative navigation and robotics systems
for orthopaedic surgery [1]–[4], for neurosurgery [5], [6], and
for radiosurgery [7], among many others. Practical, accurate,
and robust registration has emerged as one of the key technical
challenges of CAS.

content.thinking:
Livyatan 2003 is a strong primary-text addition: gradient-based 2D/3D rigid registration with a "funnelling" 3-stage pipeline (initial pose → coarse contour/geometry → fine GPR on edge pixels), "narrow convergence range" acknowledged for the fine stage, volume gradients to eliminate outliers, TRE 0.5–1.7 mm mean. This is the "gradient-on-edge-pixels" strategy in the 2D/3D fluoroscopy domain — a 2003 in-corpus precedent for the polish's edge-pixel gradient, and the "funnelling" framing matches the DIRECT→polish cascade.

I now have all the research I need. Let me also double check the Yamazaki details I want to cite: "ten different points of depth position given [over] mm steps" — the step width is missing (embedded image, "mm steps" text lost). The synthesis said "10 points over mm steps" and angle 03 R3-2 says order-4. Fine — I'll cite "ten points" + "order 4 saturated at ~0.5 mm" which are verbatim.

One more check for the survey: is there any in-corpus evidence for the "visibility gradients" claim about the 4×4 (round 1 unresolved)? Yes — the paper itself says "the optimization succeeds even at 4×4 resolution, where the average size of a rendered triangle is approximately half a pixel" — this is about tiny image resolutions, not "4×4 tiles". I can now resolve the round-1 "could not be verified" item.

Also, one more dispatch item: "does the DiffDRR family change the 'no torch in the cost path' boundary?" — My analysis:
1. DiffDRR = torch rewrite of Siddon (vectorized tensor ops). LEAP = C++/CUDA core + thin torch.nn.Module binding. Both keep the actual computation outside... no wait, DiffDRR does the computation IN torch (vectorized tensor ops + autodiff). LEAP does it in CUDA with torch only as binding.
2. For JTML: the polish's analytic gradient needs no autodiff at all — the Jacobian is closed-form. So the boundary is untouched by the DiffDRR family: the family exists precisely because low-level CUDA generators "do not offer a straightforward way to obtain gradients" — JTML's analytic route IS the low-level answer to that same problem (hand-derived Jacobians instead of autodiff).
3. The DRR channel (z-line-integral) is the ML pathway's territory; if that pathway ever needs gradients, the DiffDRR/LEAP pattern (CUDA core + thin autograd binding) is the documented engineering pattern — still outside the cost path; the "no torch in the cost path" convention concerns the DIRECT_DILATION production cost, which stays torch-free. So: no change to the boundary; the family supplies reference implementations for the ML pathway and re-confirms the matched-projector doctrine for the analytic arm.
4. Interesting nuance: DiffDRR's paper documents Nelder-Mead as the standard gradient-free DRR optimizer and the local-convexity of ZNCC — this is evidence for (a) the simplex arm in the ablation and (b) the gradient-polish premise (locally convex surrogate in the basin).

Now let me also reconsider the "simplex-polish alternative" design concretely, since the dispatch asks to re-evaluate the MVP's gradient choice against a cheap simplex-polish alternative and to include a simplex arm "if the surrogate valley is shallow":

- The simplex arm: NM on the chamfer surrogate, 7-point simplex (6-DoF + 1). Per iteration: 1-2 surrogate evals (reflection; expansion/contraction on acceptance). Termination: simplex spread < threshold (Mahfouz's criterion) or budget. Determinism: NM is deterministic given the initial simplex (fixed reflection/expansion/contraction coefficients — no randomness); the chamfer surrogate is deterministic; so the arm is rerun_identical-safe with an ordered float sum (the surrogate value itself uses int atomicAdd — deterministic). No gradient kernel, no h-calibration, no barycentric staging. Implementation: ~150-200 lines host code + the existing ChamferSurrogate wrapper (shared with the FD arm).
- When does the simplex arm make sense? The dispatch: "if the surrogate valley is shallow". The precondition gate (G1-G4) measures valley depth. A shallow, noisy (jagged, per Yamazaki) z-valley is exactly where first-order gradient steps stall (α-exhaustion) while NM's reflection/contraction can still make progress because it adapts its simplex size to the local landscape and doesn't need a gradient direction at all. Also the T=0 NM finding from Mahfouz (gradient-descent-like local search from far starts falls into nearest local minimum) is about FAR starts; the polish starts near the basin, so plain NM (T=0) is appropriate — and the Mahfouz convergence tests (final differences almost independent of initial deviation, 0.4/0.1 mm-ish) are evidence NM converges tightly in the basin.
- Cost parity: NM ~1-2 evals/iteration; at B_p = 1000, ~500-1000 NM iterations vs FD's ~140 steps / analytic's ~500 steps. NM is competitive on evals with the analytic arm (both ~1 eval per iteration) with zero gradient machinery.
- So the pre-registered design change: extend the three-arm study to a FOUR-arm study (or add simplex as a variant of arm C): A DIRECT@35k, B DIRECT@34k, C DIRECT@34k + gradient-polish@1000 (FD or analytic), D DIRECT@34k + simplex-polish@1000 (NM on the chamfer surrogate). D's inclusion is pre-registered conditional on... actually the dispatch says "the ablation arm should include a simplex arm if the surrogate valley is shallow" — the honest design: include D unconditionally in the matrix (it's cheap: same wrapper, no new kernels) and pre-register the interpretation: if G1-G4 pass, the expectation is C ≥ D on the in-plane axes (gradient's advantage: uses ∇D information); if G1 fails (shallow z valley), the expectation flips: D ≥ C on z and possibly on total cost (NM's size-adaptation beats a stalling sign-step), and the z-gap claim stays gated. Also D is the "polish without any gradient" control that isolates the value of the gradient itself vs the value of "more local search with the same budget" — a cleaner version of the B-arm control at the polish stage level. That's a genuinely useful addition: C vs D at equal polish budget isolates the gradient's marginal value.

Actually wait — there's an important subtlety: the B arm controls for the budget gift at the DIRECT level. C vs D controls for the polish mechanism (gradient vs derivative-free) at equal budget. Both are needed. D also has lineage: Mahfouz's SA-NM is the paper's own optimizer; the repo's DIRECT_MAHFOUZ diverged from SA but NM-as-polish is a cheap faithful remnant of the lineage; and the DiffDRR paper shows NM was the community-standard DRR optimizer until differentiable DRRs arrived.

- One more check: does NM need the surrogate to be smooth? NM works on non-smooth functions (it's derivative-free); on the piecewise-constant production cost it would also work but stall on plateaus; on the chamfer surrogate (Lipschitz, quantized ±1 per px) NM is well-behaved. The quantization floor (8e-4) is below NM's practical convergence tolerance; the simplex spread termination criterion (Mahfouz: best-worst < threshold) matches the polish's needs.

Now the Yamazaki-z interaction with the z-depth-channel NO-GO: 
- Yamazaki's remedy is curve-fit on the z-evaluation curve using ONLY the 2D silhouette (RMSD over projected contours) — no depth channel, no DRR, no gradient of a z-term. So a dedicated z-polish paper does NOT use any gradient-type z remedy; it uses a decoupled 1-D search with polynomial fitting. This CONFIRMS the round-1 NO-GO (no depth channel anywhere) AND refines the polish z-arm: instead of relying on the analytic gradient's z-component (which fights a distance-dependent scale and a jagged curve), the z axis should be polished by the Yamazaki-style decoupled polynomial fit (angle 03's yamazaki-polynomial mode), possibly as the terminal z-arm of the polish stage. The gradient polish handles the in-plane 5 DOF; the z-axis gets the curve-fit treatment. This is a significant upgrade to the MVP spec: a two-part polish (gradient on in-plane DOFs, Yamazaki-decoupled z-fit), matching the field's evidence (5 DOF simultaneous via nonlinear least squares + z separately — Yamazaki's own pipeline: "simultaneous optimization based on the nonlinear least-square method... and then utilizing our proposed depth position improvement technique"; and the re-registration second pass).
- The "jagged and less pointy" z curve + "gradient of the curve changed markedly with distance between X-ray focus and the model" is primary-text grounding for the R2-1 precondition-gate concern (G2 is a real empirical question at dilation 1) — Yamazaki's measurements on the SAME anatomy class (knee implants, single-plane fluoroscopy) show the z evaluation curve is the jagged one. That raises the prior on G1-G4 outcomes: the chamfer z-valley may be jagged at the 1-mm sweep step; the valley_depth formula (max−cost(0))/(max−min) absorbs jaggedness somewhat; but the G1 threshold 0.10 is a weak bar; the G2 comparison vs the dilated-overlap is the discriminating one — Yamazaki's "less pointy" note says the z-curve's peak is flat → valley depth may be modest → G2 may fail → the pre-registered z-claim semantics handle it.
- The focus→COG ray direction: Yamazaki moves the model along the ray joining the focus to the model's COG (maximal scale change per depth step). The JTML leaf z axis is the camera axis; for a centered implant these coincide; for an off-center implant the difference is the off-axis angle. Spec addition: the polish's z-perturbation direction and the probe's sweep direction should use the focus→COG ray (or record the angle) — cheap, primary-text-grounded.

Now the corpus survey ranking table (dispatch item 1):
Ranked by implementation cost against JTML's hand-written CUDA silhouette rasterizer (cheapest first):
1. Analytic edge-pixel gradient (Modular Primitives' rasterizer backward, rigid-body reduction) — the MVP's own design; verified in-corpus: (ID,u,v,zc/wc) output, scatter-add backward, AA-as-separate-stage; the MVP saves the Juv term and the vertex scatter (rigid body). Cost: the staged barycentrics sibling kernel (~10 lines) + ChamferGradientKernel (~50 lines). This is the cheapest *gradient* strategy because it reuses the existing fill's barycentrics and needs no changes to the forward image.
2. Forward-projection/differentiable-DRR (DiffDRR/LEAP): applies to the DRR path; the codebase already has the DRR fill + z-line-integral; making it differentiable = analytic Jacobians of the ray-casting (Siddon-style) or autodiff (torch — NO-GO). Cheaper than soft-rasterizer/SDF routes in principle (the forward model exists) but gated by the photometric NO-GO (saturated implant → no intensity gradient; and it's the ML pathway, not the polish). Not the polish's strategy.
3. Soft-rasterizer coverage (SoftRas): per-triangle probabilistic coverage maps + depth-ordered softmax aggregation → reworks the fill's output semantics fundamentally (per-triangle contributions instead of last-writer-wins); SoftRas tests "each triangle for every pixel" (Modular Primitives' critique) — the opposite of JTML's fragment-stream design; plus the blur-vs-correctness tuning (field's own critique). Cost: high (~2-4 weeks), fallback-only.
4. SDF reparameterization (Bangaru 2022; Wang 2024): requires an SDF representation + ray marching/sphere tracing + warp construction — all absent from the codebase; for a fixed STL this is pure overhead. Cost: highest; N/A for the MVP.
5. Edge-sampling / boundary-integral (PSDR/Zhang 2020; Li et al.): in PBR the boundary integral needs MC sampling with silhouette detection ("do not scale well to complex geometry due to the necessity for run-time silhouette detection"); in the rasterization context the practical boundary handling is Modular Primitives' analytic AA (the documented fallback), and the MVP's FD-twin gate decides whether the boundary term needs handling at all. Cost: medium as the AA fallback; high as a PBR-style MC sampler (N/A).
6. Topological derivatives (Mehta 2023): level-set surface evolution with hole/phase nucleation — for topology-changing shape reconstruction; a rigid 6-DoF pose has no topology changes. N/A (theory note: visibility terms in shape derivatives are evaluated only on apparent contours — matching the MVP's contour-only gradient).

So the ranking: analytic edge-pixel (MVP) < forward-projection (DRR path, ML pathway) < soft coverage < edge-sampling-AA (fallback) < SDF reparam ≈ pathspace ≈ topological (N/A). And the cheapest of ALL is the derivative-free simplex (no gradient at all) — the reason the ablation gains arm D.

The "no torch in the cost path" boundary: unchanged by the DiffDRR family — DiffDRR solves "CUDA generators don't give gradients" by rewriting in torch; JTML's analytic Jacobian solves the same problem without torch; LEAP documents the CUDA-core + thin-binding pattern as the alternative (which JTML's "no torch" convention already matches); the family's references are for the ML/DRR pathway (outside the cost path by construction).

## Round 3 — The corpus survey, the simplex precedent, and the Yamazaki z-polish (final deepening)

### Summary

This round moved the polish MVP's evidence base onto the in-library primary texts and changed two design decisions. (1) The corpus survey ranks the five gradient strategies against JTML's hand-written CUDA rasterizer: the analytic edge-pixel gradient (the R2-4 design) is confirmed the cheapest — Modular Primitives (now in-corpus) is literally a rasterizer + pixel-dense scatter-add backward, of which the MVP is the rigid-body reduction — while SoftRas coverage, SDF reparameterization, path-space edge sampling, and topological derivatives are all more expensive or N/A for a fixed-STL 6-DoF pose; the DiffDRR family does NOT change the 'no torch in the cost path' boundary (DiffDRR exists precisely because low-level generators lack gradients — the analytic Jacobian is the low-level answer; LEAP documents the CUDA-core-plus-thin-binding pattern JTML already matches). (2) The simplex precedent is real and the MVP design changes: Mahfouz 2003's optimizer IS a 7-point Nelder-Mead simplex with SA temperature (the repo dropped the SA, the simplex remains the cheapest polish of all), and DiffDRR's paper documents Nelder-Mead as the community-standard DRR optimizer — so the ablation gains a FOURTH arm D (Nelder-Mead simplex polish on the chamfer surrogate, B_p = 1000, zero gradient machinery), and C-vs-D at equal polish budget becomes the cleanest isolate of the gradient's marginal value. (3) Yamazaki 2004 is geometry/curve-fit, not gradient-type: a decoupled order-4 polynomial fit over 10 depth samples along the focus→COG ray — confirming the z-depth-channel NO-GO (no depth channel anywhere; z is purely silhouette-scale) and upgrading the polish's z-arm to the decoupled Yamazaki-style fit as a terminal stage. (4) The round-2 pull list re-ranks: SoftRas, Modular Primitives, DiffDRR, LEAP, and Gablonsky 2001 are now in-library (superseded as pulls); NVDiffrast/GitHub, arXiv:1906.07870, and Veriserum remain the only still-necessary pulls.

Key findings:

**R3-1 — The corpus survey: the analytic edge-pixel gradient is the cheapest strategy, and the reference implementation is now in-library (with two round-1/2 open items resolved)**
- Verification of the R2-3/R2-4 design against the primary text (laineModularPrimitivesHighPerformance2020.txt, in-corpus): the rasterizer forward outputs "a 2D sample grid, with each position storing a tuple (ID, u, v, zc/wc)" (L549-552) with "a buffer with the 2×2 Jacobian of the barycentrics w.r.t. the screen coordinates Juv = ∂{u,v}/∂{x,y}" (L561-562); the backward is "a dense operation over output pixels, using a scatter-add operation to accumulate the gradients from the pixels to the correct vertices based on the triangle IDs" (L589-594); analytic AA is a SEPARATE post-shading stage ("point-sampled visibility causes aliasing at visibility discontinuities, and more crucially, cannot produce visibility-related gradients for vertex positions. Antialiasing converts the discontinuities to smooth changes") (L751-762) — exactly the R2-4 structure (pixel-grid kernel + ordered reduction + optional boundary/AA fallback). [Source: corpus — l/laineModularPrimitivesHighPerformance2020.txt]
- RESOLVED (round-1/2 open item): the z/w no-gradient policy is IN THE PAPER, not just GitHub issue #70: "The NDC depth is utilized only by the subsequent antialiasing module, and does not propagate gradients" (L558-560). The round-1 "issue #70 search-verified only" caveat is closed by the primary text; the GitHub issue retains only the verbatim-issue-text value. [Source: corpus — l/laineModularPrimitivesHighPerformance2020.txt L558-560]
- RESOLVED (round-1 open item): the "4×4" claim is a tiny-image-resolution stress test, not a tile size: "To our surprise, the optimization succeeds even at 4×4 resolution, where the average size of a rendered triangle is approximately half a pixel" (L920-924) — the visibility-gradient pipeline works at sub-pixel triangle sizes; at 2×2 it fails (L903-904). Round 1's "could not be verified" item is now resolved against the primary text. [Source: corpus — l/laineModularPrimitivesHighPerformance2020.txt L903-904, L920-924]
- Ranking of the five dispatch-named strategies by implementation cost against the JTML rasterizer (cheapest first): (1) analytic edge-pixel gradient (Modular-Primitives-style, rigid-body reduction) — reuses the fill's existing barycentrics + static dev_triangles_; the ~10-line staged-attributes sibling kernel + ~50-line ChamferGradientKernel; NO change to forward-image semantics; (2) forward-projection / differentiable-DRR (DiffDRR/LEAP family) — the forward model exists (render_drr_engine.cu z-line-integral), but it is the ML-pathway channel, gated by the round-1 photometric NO-GO (saturated implant, no usable intensity gradient), so it is not a polish strategy; (3) soft-rasterizer coverage (SoftRas) — per-triangle probabilistic coverage maps + depth-ordered softmax aggregation (Dji = sigmoid(δji·d(i,j)/σ), silhouette AO = 1 − Π(1−Dji); L321-334, L459-469) replaces last-writer-wins with per-triangle contributions "for every pixel" — Modular Primitives' own critique: "Soft Rasterizer... tests each triangle for every pixel, and consequently loses to our method by several orders of magnitude" (L1250-1253), and the blur "makes opaque surfaces become transparent around edges, leading to an incorrect image. Optimization thus requires tuning these parameters" (L259-263) — a fundamental rework, fallback-only; (4) edge-sampling / boundary integral (PSDR family) — in the PBR context needs MC sampling with runtime silhouette detection that "does not scale well to complex geometry" (zhangPathspaceDifferentiableRendering2020.txt L632-637); the rasterization-adjacent form is Modular Primitives' analytic AA (the documented fallback), and the R2-4 FD-twin gate decides whether the boundary term needs it at all; (5) SDF reparameterization (Bangaru 2022 / Wang 2024) — requires an SDF representation + sphere tracing/ray marching + warp construction absent from the codebase; for a fixed STL this is pure overhead (the strategy exists for shape-DEFORMATION and neural-SDF reconstruction); topological derivatives (Mehta 2023) — level-set evolution with hole/phase nucleation for topology-changing reconstruction; a rigid 6-DoF pose has no topology changes, N/A (one theory note: "visibility terms in SDs are evaluated only on the apparent contours" (L~70) — the theory-level confirmation that contour-only gradients are the norm for visibility, matching the MVP's EDGE-set-only gradient). [Sources: corpus — l/liuSoftRasterizerDifferentiable2019.txt, l/laineModularPrimitivesHighPerformance2020.txt, z/zhangPathspaceDifferentiableRendering2020.txt, b/bangaruDifferentiableRenderingNeural2022.txt, w/wangSimpleApproachDifferentiable2024.txt, m/mehtaTheoryTopologicalDerivatives2023.txt]
- A 2003 in-corpus clinical precedent for the edge-pixel gradient strategy: Livyatan et al. "Gradient-Based 2-D/3-D Rigid Registration of Fluoroscopic X-Ray to CT" (TMI 22(11), livyatanGradientbased2D3D2003.txt) — a three-stage "funnelling" pipeline (initial pose → coarse contour-based → fine "gradient projection registration (GPR) on edge pixels"), the fine stage explicitly "has a narrow convergence range" (L273-274, L302) — i.e., a DIRECT-like coarse stage + edge-pixel-gradient fine stage is exactly the polish's architecture, field-validated in 2D/3D fluoroscopy registration for two decades, with mean TRE 0.5–1.7 mm. [Source: corpus — l/livyatanGradientbased2D3D2003.txt L13-14, L273-274, L302]
- Confidence: high (all primary texts read directly this round; the ranking is an implementation-cost judgment grounded in the verified kernel facts from rounds 1-2).
- Relevance to this project: answers dispatch item (1) — the MVP's analytic design is the cheapest gradient strategy in the set; nothing in the corpus upgrades SoftRas/SDF/PSDR from fallback/N-A status; two round-1/2 "could not be verified" items are closed.

**R3-2 — The DiffDRR family does NOT change the 'no torch in the cost path' boundary — it confirms it, and supplies two pieces of polish evidence**
- DiffDRR (gopalakrishnanFastAutoDifferentiableDigitally2022.txt, in-corpus) exists because "most DRR generators do not offer a straightforward way to obtain gradients" (L22-23) — the paper's solution is to reformulate Siddon's method as vectorized tensor ops in PyTorch and lean on autodiff. The polish's analytic 2×6 projection Jacobian is the low-level answer to the same problem, with no autodiff anywhere — so the family's existence is evidence FOR the boundary, not against it: JTML already has what DiffDRR had to build torch to get. [Source: corpus — g/gopalakrishnanFastAutoDifferentiableDigitally2022.txt L22-28]
- LEAP (kimDifferentiableForwardProjector2023.txt, in-corpus) is the alternative engineering pattern: "core C++/CUDA module, Python binding and PyTorch interfaces" (L183-185, L236-241) — torch as a thin binding over a hand-written CUDA core, in XCT (voxel line integrals), NOT silhouette registration. The matched-projector doctrine is verbatim: "one should employ methods for backprojection that are the exact transpose of the forward projection, referred to as matched projectors... stable after over a thousand or more iterations, we chose to implement methods where the exact transpose is used" (L210-221) — the R2-4 gradient-twin gate is the rasterization-side implementation of this doctrine (the analytic gradient must equal the FD twin of the same forward). [Source: corpus — k/kimDifferentiableForwardProjector2023.txt L183-185, L210-221]
- Two polish-relevant findings inside DiffDRR: (a) the community baseline before differentiable DRRs was Nelder-Mead: "many applications use iterative gradient-free methods, such as the Nelder-Mead method [11], to optimize an image similarity metric" (L64-66) — primary-text support for the simplex arm (R3-3); (b) "the loss landscapes for slice-to-volume registration in particular is convex in a large region around the optimum, making this problem better suited for gradient-based optimization methods" (L67-68), measured for negative ZNCC over ±30 mm / ±90° (L360-370) — the field's measured evidence that image-similarity landscapes are locally convex in the basin, the premise the polish's surrogate-gradient relies on. Their 6-DoF gradient descent used per-axis update rates "because they have different units (βθϕγ = 5.3×10⁻² and βxyz = 7.5×10¹), and momentum λ = 0.9" (L628-630) — primary-text confirmation of the per-axis-scaling necessity (the h·sign(g) / ADAM-lite design, R2-2/R2-6). [Source: corpus — g/gopalakrishnanFastAutoDifferentiableDigitally2022.txt L64-68, L360-370, L628-630]
- Boundary verdict: unchanged. The convention is about the PRODUCTION cost path (DIRECT_DILATION and its metrics stay torch-free); the DRR/z-line-integral channel is the ML pathway, where the DiffDRR/LEAP pattern (hand-written CUDA core; torch only as an optional binding) is the documented reference if that pathway is ever built — same as round 1. [Source: angle 06 Round 1 "feasibility verdicts" (torch bridge NO-GO); corpus — g/gopalakrishnan..., k/kim...]
- Confidence: high.
- Relevance: answers the second half of dispatch item (1) — the boundary holds; the family adds two measured facts (locally-convex basin, NM baseline) that harden the polish's premise and its ablation design.

**R3-3 — The simplex precedent: Mahfouz's optimizer IS a 7-point Nelder-Mead simplex with SA temperature; the ablation gains arm D (plain NM polish), and C-vs-D isolates the gradient's marginal value**
- Primary text (mahfouzRobustMethodRegistration2003.txt, in-corpus): "Our SA algorithm is a modified version of the Nelder–Mead [30] (downhill simplex) optimization method. A simplex is a set of seven points where each point represents a possible pose, along with the value of the function space at that point. The algorithm iteratively perturbs the worst (highest) point of the simplex, in the direction of a lower score" (L451-454, L473-474); SA = "adds or subtracts a positive, logarithmically distributed random variable, proportional to the temperature, to the function values in the simplex" with "the temperature... decreased every 40 iterations by multiplying the current temperature by 0.99" and periodic simplex expansion (L479-488); termination "when the difference between the best and worst points in the simplex is less than a small threshold" (L490-491); ~0.2 s/iteration on a 1998 SGI Octane (L489). [Source: corpus — m/mahfouzRobustMethodRegistration2003.txt]
- The repo already dropped the SA ("Not Using Simulated Annealing Obviously..." — implant_mahfouz_metric.cu:249-251); the polish should keep it dropped: Mahfouz's own T=0 control shows why — "with temperature equal to zero, the algorithm becomes a simple gradient descent algorithm that just traverses downhill to the nearest local minimum. We found, as expected, that the algorithm quickly fell into a local minimum near its starting point" (L597-602). That is the correct behavior FOR A POLISH (the DIRECT trunk already did the basin selection; the polish must NOT escape the basin it was handed); SA's escape machinery is the global-search feature the polish deliberately does not want. Plain NM is the Mahfouz-validated local search at zero gradient cost. [Source: corpus — m/mahfouzRobustMethodRegistration2003.txt L597-602; repo — src/compute/implant_mahfouz_metric.cu:249-251]
- Design change (concrete): the R2-5 three-arm study becomes FOUR arms — D: DIRECT@34k + simplex-polish@B_p=1000, where the polish is a 7-point Nelder-Mead on the chamfer surrogate (the shared ~35-line ChamferSurrogate wrapper from R2-2, no gradient kernel, no h-calibration, no barycentric staging; standard reflection/expansion/contraction per nelderSIMPLEXMETHODFUNCTION1965.txt L40-70; the initial simplex built from the leaf-box ranges scaled by the R2-2 h defaults; termination = simplex spread < threshold (Mahfouz's criterion) or B_p exhausted; every surrogate + trial-verification eval increments cost_function_calls_ exactly as in arms B/C). Implementation: ~150-200 host lines, deterministic (no randomness — unlike Mahfouz's SA version, the polish's plain NM is RNG-free, so rerun_identical is preserved; the surrogate value path is the same int-atomic-deterministic one). [Sources: corpus — n/nelderSIMPLEXMETHODFUNCTION1965.txt L40-70, m/mahfouzRobustMethodRegistration2003.txt L451-491; angle 06 R2-2/R2-5]
- Why arm D is included UNCONDITIONALLY (the dispatch's "if the surrogate valley is shallow" is folded into the interpretation, not the inclusion): D costs one run column (~15 min/unit on the R2-5 matrix) and uses only the shared wrapper; excluding it on a predicted gate would leave the cheap control unmeasured. Pre-registered interpretation: (i) C-vs-D at equal polish budget is the cleanest isolate of the gradient's marginal value — if the surrogate valley is deep (G1-G4 pass), the expectation is C ≥ D (the gradient uses ∇D information NM lacks); if the valley is shallow (G1 fails — Yamazaki's jagged-z-curve prior, R3-4), the expectation flips: D ≥ C on the z axis and possibly on total cost, because NM's size-adapting reflection/contraction keeps making progress where a sign-step gradient stalls at the quantization floor; (ii) D-vs-B is the "local search is worth B_p evals at all" test independent of the gradient mechanism; (iii) if D ≈ C ≈ B, the polish hypothesis itself is dead at this budget — an honest null the three-arm design could not fully distinguish (C > B could have meant "local search in general helps", not "the gradient helps"). [Source: angle 06 R2-5; corpus — m/mahfouzRobustMethodRegistration2003.txt (T=0 result, L597-602)]
- Lineage note: NM-on-the-chamfer-surrogate is the closest faithful remnant of the DIRECT_MAHFOUZ lineage's optimizer (the metric's own 2003 paper used exactly a 7-point NM); the repo's divergence ("Not Using SA") is about the annealing, not the simplex — arm D completes the lineage comparison the run's Mahfouz work opened (angle 02 R3-1). [Sources: repo — src/compute/implant_mahfouz_metric.cu:249-251; corpus — m/mahfouzRobustMethodRegistration2003.txt]
- Confidence: high on the mechanics (primary text + the shared wrapper; NM is ~150 lines of textbook host code); medium on the direction of the C-vs-D comparison (that is what the arm measures).
- Relevance: answers dispatch item (2) — the simplex-polish alternative is cheaper to implement than the gradient arms (no new kernels at all), has direct lineage, and its inclusion as arm D makes the ablation's polish conclusion unambiguous about WHERE the win (if any) comes from.

**R3-4 — Yamazaki 2004: the dedicated depth-position paper uses a geometry/curve-fit remedy, not a gradient-type one — confirming the z-depth-channel NO-GO and upgrading the polish's z-arm to a decoupled fit**
- The remedy, from the primary text (yamazakiImprovementDepthPosition2004.txt): after initial 6-DoF registration (Levenberg–Marquardt — a gradient-type method for the joint problem), depth position is optimized INDEPENDENTLY: "the model is moved along a straight line... joining the X-ray focus F and the gravity center of the model G" (L265-269), the depth position sampled at "ten different points... over mm steps" (L370-371), RMSD computed at each, "the set of points... fitted to the polynomial" (L285-286), the extremum of the fitted polynomial taken as the depth optimum (L295-298), then "conventional 2-D/3-D registration was carried out a second time using the corrected depth position" (L300-302). Order selection measured: "for fourth- and higher-order polynomials, the extremum error is almost saturated (about 0.5 mm)" → order 4 (L380-383). Results: depth RMSE 2.6→0.9 mm (sim) / 3.2→1.4 mm (in vitro) (L28-29); residual ~0.5 mm bias "thought to be caused by slight errors in translation parallel to fluoroscopic images" (L629-631). NO depth channel, NO DRR, NO gradient of a z-term anywhere in the remedy — the z signal is purely the 2-D silhouette scale change ("a change in the depth position causes only small changes in the 2-D silhouette", L14-15; "the distance between the X-ray focus and the object is large, and as a result, the amount of information for changes in the projected 2-D silhouette is smaller than that for depth changes", L104-107). [Source: corpus — y/yamazakiImprovementDepthPosition2004.txt]
- Interaction with the round-1 z-depth-channel NO-GO: CONFIRMS it from inside the field's own dedicated-depth paper. Yamazaki improves z by extracting MORE from the existing single-plane silhouettes (a 10-point curve fit), not by adding any depth sensing — the "depth channel" concept (front-surface z/w buffer) would give the polish nothing to compare against, exactly as round 1 argued (no target depth in single-plane fluoro; z is magnification). The paper's mechanism quote is the 2004 version of the round-1 observability argument: z accuracy is limited by the amount of 2-D silhouette information, not by the optimizer. [Source: corpus — y/yamazakiImprovementDepthPosition2004.txt L104-107; angle 06 Round 1 "depth channel" finding]
- Three spec changes the primary text forces: (a) the polish's z-arm should be the DECOUPLED Yamazaki-style fit, not the gradient's z-component: "the evaluation curve for depth position was more jagged, and the curve peak less pointy" (L20-21, L620-621) and "the gradient of the curve changed markedly with distance between X-ray focus and the model" (L621-623) → "it is difficult to find an appropriate scale for depth position" (L626) — this is the primary-text version of the R2-1 G2 concern AND of the SAME_Z fixed-weight problem (a fixed z-weight fights a distance-dependent z-gradient scale; Yamazaki's fit "does not require adjustment of the weight value" (L353-355)). Concretely: the polish runs the gradient/simplex on the 5 in-plane DOFs + z jointly OR on 5 DOF with z handled by the probe's yamazaki-polynomial mode (order-4 fit on the SAME 31-render sweep, angle 03 R3-2) as the terminal z stage — the ablation compares SAME_Z-weighted vs decoupled (already angle 03 R3-2's axis; the primary text now supplies the mechanism). (b) The sweep/perturbation direction should be the focus→COG ray, not the camera-z axis: for a centered implant these coincide; for an off-center implant the leaf z-axis differs by the off-axis angle — the R2-2 h_z = 8 mm default and the probe's ±15 mm sweep both assume camera-z; record the off-axis angle and (cheap) use the ray direction. (c) The "jagged" z-curve prior feeds the precondition gate: G1's 0.10 valley-depth threshold is the right weak bar (a jagged-but-V-shaped curve still passes), and G2 (chamfer vs dilated) remains the discriminating gate — exactly the R2-1 design, now with a primary-text prior that the z curve is the jagged one in THIS anatomy class. [Sources: corpus — y/yamazakiImprovementDepthPosition2004.txt L20-21, L352-355, L620-626; angle 03 R3-2; angle 06 R2-1/R2-2]
